Diwali historical origin: Diwali is one of India's most widely celebrated festivals and has several regional religious narratives. In many North Indian traditions it is associated with Rama's return to Ayodhya after exile and victory over Ravana. Other traditions connect the festival with Lakshmi, Krishna's victory over Narakasura, Govardhan Puja and King Bali. The common symbolic theme is light overcoming darkness, good overcoming evil and renewal.

How celebrated: Cooking Pongal outdoors, drawing kolam, decorating cattle, family gatherings and visiting relatives. Contemporary celebration: Sun worship, Pongal offering, cattle worship and ceremonial cooking. Observance timing: Thai month; usually January 14–17. (duration: 4 days). Pongal historical origin: Pongal is a major Tamil harvest festival celebrating the agricultural cycle and expressing gratitude to the Sun, nature, farmers and cattle. The name comes from the Tamil word pongu, meaning to boil over or overflow. The overflowing rice dish symbolizes abundance and prosperity. The festival developed around Tamil agrarian life and continues today as a four-day celebration involving Bhogi, Thai Pongal, Mattu Pongal and Kaanum Pongal.

Holi historical origin: Holi is the Hindu festival of colours and spring. One important religious tradition connects Holika Dahan with the story of Prahlada and Holika, symbolizing the victory of devotion and good over destructive power. Another tradition connects the colourful celebration with Krishna and Radha. Over time, Holi also became a major social festival associated with forgiveness, friendship and renewal.

Maha Shivaratri historical origin: Maha Shivaratri is the great night dedicated to Shiva. Hindu traditions associate the festival with several sacred narratives, including Shiva's cosmic significance and, in some traditions, the marriage of Shiva and Parvati. Devotees traditionally stay awake during the night, worship Shiva and perform abhishekam.

Ramadan historical origin: Ramadan is the ninth month of the Islamic Hijri calendar and is the month in which Muslims commemorate the beginning of the revelation of the Qur'an to Prophet Muhammad through the Angel Jibril (Gabriel).
According to Islamic tradition, the revelation began during Laylat al-Qadr, the Night of Decree, in Ramadan. The month therefore became a period of fasting, worship, Qur'an recitation, charity, self-discipline and spiritual reflection.
Fasting during Ramadan is one of the Five Pillars of Islam. From dawn until sunset, adult Muslims who are able are expected to abstain from food and drink, as well as other prohibited actions, while increasing prayer, charity and remembrance of Allah.

Ninth month of the Hijri calendar.

Eid-ul-Zuha (Eid-ul-Azha) is a major Festival in Islam. Marked by the ritual sacrifice of a goat, or bakra, symbolising devotion and obedience to Allah. Significance: Emphasizes devotion, generosity, charity and community. Coincides with the Hajj pilgrimage. How celebrated: Sacrificial meat is shared among family, friends, and the less fortunate, with a third reserved for those in need. Contemporary celebration: Modern celebrations vary according to local law and custom. Observance timing: 10 Dhu-al-Hijjah (duration: Several days). Regions: Global Muslim communities.
Eid-ul-Zuha (Eid-ul-Azha) historical origin: Honours the Prophet Ibrahim's unwavering faith, which Allah tested by instructing him to sacrifice his son.

Milad-Un-Nabi is a major Festival in Islam. A solemn celebration of the birth anniversary of the Prophet Muhammad. Significance: Recognised as a day of respect and modest festivities, honouring the Prophet's virtues. How celebrated: People gather in mosques for Quranic recitations, reciting the Qasida al-Burda Sharif and Nats. Contemporary celebration: In Kashmir, devotees visit the Hazratbal Shrine in Srinagar. Observance timing: 12 Rabi-al-Awwal (duration: 1 day). Regions: Global Muslim communities.
Milad-Un-Nabi historical origin: The Prophet was born on the twelfth day of Rabi-al-Awwal, a date also believed to mark his passing.

Muharram is a major Observance in Islam. Honours the martyrdom of Hussain, the son of Ali and grandson of the Prophet Muhammad. Significance: A solemn occasion and the Islamic New Year, marked globally as a day of mourning by Shia Muslims. How celebrated: Tajia processions, wearing black as a sign of grief, and distributing sherbet or juice to the public. Contemporary celebration: Modern observance is highly dependent on local tradition. Observance timing: 1st month of Islamic calendar (duration: 10 days (Yaum-al-Ashura)). Regions: Global Muslim communities.
Muharram historical origin: Remembering Hussain's sacrifice at the Battle of Karbala in 680 AD (61 Hijri).

Christmas historical origin: Christmas commemorates the birth of Jesus Christ. According to the New Testament, Jesus was born to Mary in Bethlehem. The Gospel accounts describe Mary and Joseph travelling to Bethlehem, where Jesus was born and laid in a manger because there was no suitable lodging available.
The birth of Jesus became central to Christian belief because Christians understand him as the Son of God and the promised Messiah. The Gospel of Luke describes angels announcing the birth to shepherds, while Matthew describes visitors from the East bringing gifts.
The Christian celebration of Christmas developed over the centuries. December 25 became an established date for the celebration in the Western Christian tradition, while some Eastern Christian communities follow different calendar traditions. Christmas gradually developed from a primarily religious observance into a major cultural celebration involving family gatherings, gifts, charitable activities, music and decorations.

Origin: Christian celebration of the Nativity of Jesus.

The festival occurs during the annual Hajj pilgrimage and is closely connected with the story of Ibrahim, his family and their devotion to Allah.

Islamic New Year historical origin: The Islamic calendar is a lunar calendar beginning with Muharram.

Navratri historical origin: Navratri means “nine nights” and is a major festival devoted to Shakti, the divine feminine. A major tradition associates Sharad Navratri with the battle between Goddess Durga and Mahishasura and her victory over him. However, Navratri takes different forms throughout India, including Garba in Gujarat, Durga Puja in Bengal, Ramlila in North India and Golu in Tamil Nadu.

The festival became especially prominent as a large public celebration in Maharashtra during the modern period, although Ganesha worship is much older. Public celebrations combine religious worship with community and cultural activities.

Janmashtami is a major Festival in Hinduism. The celebration of the birth of Lord Krishna, observed with devotion, music and midnight prayers. Significance: Celebrates Krishna's birth and his divine qualities of love, wisdom and protection of dharma. How celebrated: Devotees fast until midnight, participate in bhajans and kirtans, perform Dahi Handi (a human pyramid to break a pot of curd, symbolising Krishna's love of butter), and celebrate with midnight prayers. Contemporary celebration: Celebrated globally, with ISKCON temples hosting large events; Dahi Handi is a major public event in Maharashtra. Observance timing: Bhadrapada Krishna Ashtami (August) (duration: 1–2 days). Regions: India.

Janmashtami historical origin: Janmashtami commemorates the birth of Krishna at midnight in Mathura. Texts describe his birth as the eighth avatar of Vishnu. The Braj region (Mathura, Vrindavan) has the oldest and most elaborate celebrations.

Rama Navami historical origin: Rama Navami celebrates the birth of Lord Rama according to the Ramayana tradition. Rama is presented in Hindu tradition as an embodiment of dharma and righteous kingship. Devotees therefore use the festival to remember Rama's virtues and teachings.

Many historical and legendary narratives have become a... Significance: Blessings, protection and family bonds. Celebrates brother-sister relationships. Raksha Bandhan historical origin: Raksha Bandhan is a festival celebrating sibling affection and the symbolic bond of protection. Many historical and legendary narratives have become associated with the practice, but the exact historical origin is not represented by a single universally accepted event. Today the central custom is the tying of rakhi.

Dussehra historical origin: Vijayadashami marks victory over evil in several Hindu traditions. In the Ramayana tradition it commemorates Rama's victory over Ravana, while Shakta traditions associate the day with Durga's victory over Mahishasura. Therefore, the exact story and celebration differ regionally, but the broad theme is the triumph of dharma over adharma.

The festival combines seasonal celebration with educational and religious traditions. In many communities, children are introduced to learning or writing during the festival.

Guru Purnima historical origin: Guru Purnima is a day dedicated to honouring teachers and spiritual guides. It is traditionally associated with Vyasa and is therefore sometimes called Vyasa Purnima. The wider concept celebrates the transmission of knowledge from teacher to student.

Karwa Chauth historical origin: Karwa Chauth is a traditional fasting observance practiced particularly by married women in parts of North and Northwest India. Its customs developed through regional marital and devotional traditions. The fast is associated with prayers for the wellbeing and longevity of one's husband, while modern observances increasingly emphasize family relationships and mutual affection.

Makara Sankranti is a major Festival in Hinduism. A harvest festival marking the sun's transition into Capricorn, celebrated across India with regional names. Significance: A time of harvest thanksgiving; regarded as auspicious for holy dips, charity and worship. Also celebrated as Pongal in Tamil Nadu and Lohri in Punjab. How celebrated: Ritual dips in sacred rivers, flying kites (especially in Gujarat), preparing til-gul (sesame and jaggery sweets), and Pongal rice dishes.
